title: Bruhn–Rautenbach's Fano-plane determinant conjecture
source: Igor Araujo, József Balogh and Yuzhou Wang, “Maximum determinant and permanent of sparse 0-1 matrices”, arXiv:2011.01892 (2020), Section 6; Linear Algebra Appl. 645 (2022) 194–228. The conjecture goes back to Bruhn and Rautenbach, “Maximal determinants of combinatorial matrices”, arXiv:1711.09935, Linear Algebra Appl. (2018). https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01892

significance.root_decision: Every n×n 0-1 matrix with at most 3n ones satisfies |det A|^7 ≤ 24^n, so det A ≤ 24^(n/7), with equality for disjoint unions of Fano incidence matrices. The best published bounds were 2^(2n/3) (Araujo, Balogh and Wang) and 24^(n/6) (Scheinerman). The proof normalizes the matrix on both sides by its row and column degrees, bounds the logarithm of the determinant of the normalized Gram matrix through its trace and the trace of its square with degree-dependent centres (an integer-degree envelope that is sharp exactly at degree three), and closes with a linear edge/vertex potential that survives deletion of rows and columns of degree one; the induction runs on the potential bound, which needs no density hypothesis, so a deletion that raises the density is harmless. Lean proves the integer form |det A|^7 ≤ 24^n and derives the printed real-power form, and checks that the Fano matrix (21 ones, determinant 24) attains equality and that the hypotheses are satisfiable for every n.
significance.caveat: The journal texts (LAA 2018 and 2022) were not read in full (publisher and NSF copies refused or failed); the indexed journal passages still state the conjecture, and every later paper found calls it open. Cross-model confidence 0.9, not routine 0.85. No second cross-model lane read the finished Lean: root compared the final theorem and every definition with the endpoint the Claude Opus reviewer had written (identical), and the GPT-6.1 Sol final check compared the statement with both source papers and reran the scalar inequalities, the Fano case and an exhaustive check for n ≤ 5.
